extracted.intended_audience: researchers, practitioners, policymakers, and students interested in disinformation, fellowship applicants, and potential partners
extracted.subtask_description: A program page describing the Assembly: Disinformation initiative at the Berkman Klein Center, its organization into three tracks (Forum, Student Fellowship, Assembly Fellowship), goals, participant makeup, activities, and outputs. Useful for prospective fellows, partners, and stakeholders learning what the program expects and produces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant composition (cross-sector, multidisciplinary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brings together participants from academia, industry, government, and civil society from across disciplines to explore and make progress on disinformation in the digital public sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program design emphasizes diverse, cross-sector participation to surface multiple perspectives and practical approaches to disinformation problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of topics addressed
rubrics_metrics.description: Addresses the challenges and opportunities of public and private sector responses to disinformation and related problems, including within cybersecurity, platforms and internet governance, public health, politics, elections, democracy, and public discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work and projects should engage with one or more of these substantive domains and understand their intersections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-interest focus and cross-sectoral collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Brings together innovative approaches to cross-sectoral collaborations focused on the public interest and thoughtful interdisciplinary programming, with the Berkman Klein Center's history as a convener and long view on the problems and promise of the internet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects and activities are expected to prioritize the public interest rather than narrow commercial aims and to use cross-sector partnerships to increase impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program structure: three tracks
rubrics_metrics.description: The program is organized around three tracks: the Assembly Forum, the Assembly Student Fellowship, and the Assembly Fellowship. The tracks are designed to bring together cohorts of experts, professionals, and students to better understand, and actively address, complex issues of disinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each track serves a distinct audience and function (senior leadership discussion, student cohort learning, practitioner project development); applicants/participants should select the track matching their role and goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assembly Forum: senior leadership discussion under Chatham House Rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The Assembly Forum is a discussion forum for senior leadership from internet platforms, the government, the academic field, and civil society. It hosts briefings and conversations conducted under the Chatham House Rule on specific challenges and solutions for disinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forum participation emphasizes candid exchange, making connections across sectors, surfacing agreement, making progress on hard problems, and offering recommendations where pertinent; confidentiality (Chatham House Rule) is used to elicit candid perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assembly Student Fellowship design and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Brings together a cohort of Harvard students from a range of disciplines and schools who participate in problem-oriented seminars led by Harvard faculty, practitioners, and experts, and engage in active discussion about disinformation problems in the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Student fellows engage with a range of topics (disinformation and election security, race and racism, public health, platform policies, journalism) and are expected to participate in seminars and discussions oriented toward problem-solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assembly Fellowship design and deliverables
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-residential four-month fellowship for technologists, scholars, and policymakers. Assembly Fellows develop projects and prototypes aimed at addressing challenges related to the year’s theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fellows are expected to learn and build together with a deep focus on the public interest; projects should produce prototypes or actionable interventions and fellows are encouraged to apply their learnings to ongoing work after the fellowship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of projects, prototypes, and public outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Assembly Fellows develop projects and prototypes; the program showcases work (e.g., project showcases, publications, video series) and produces resources such as the US Elections Disinformation Tabletop Exercise Package intended for stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outputs are intended for practical use by stakeholders (intelligence community, social media companies, election officials, news media) and should be actionable and audience-targeted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on interdisciplinary, collaborative problem-solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Assembly is collaborative by design and builds on existing research, including previous Center work on intermediary responsibility, cybersecurity, the media ecosystem, and their intersections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful projects and discussions integrate multiple disciplines and draw on prior research and programmatic experience to address complex, intersecting issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program goals: eliciting candid perspectives and making progress on hard problems
rubrics_metrics.description: The Forum aims to elicit candid perspectives, surface points of agreement, make progress on hard problems, and offer recommendations where pertinent. The program sees tackling disinformation as a forcing function for conversations on trust and responsibility in the information ecosystem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activities should produce substantive insights, points of consensus where possible, and practical recommendations rather than purely academic discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target audiences for exercises and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain program outputs (e.g., tabletop exercises) are explicitly designed for particular stakeholders such as the intelligence community, social media companies, state election officials, and news media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design of exercises/resources should consider the operational needs and roles of these stakeholder groups to be practically useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity with prior programs and thematic focus
rubrics_metrics.description: These three tracks build on existing work, including programs formerly known as the Berklett Cybersecurity project, Techtopia, and the Assembly program (a joint initiative with the MIT Media Lab). From 2019-2021 the Assembly Fellowship focused on addressing disinformation on online platforms; in previous years the program addressed digital privacy and security, and ethics and governance of AI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants and participants should align projects with the program’s current thematic focus while recognizing the program’s evolving history and past emphases.
